new.analysis:
## What happened
None of the three walk-runs planned for Sep 21 – 27 were logged. Your check-in says your sleep, stress and body all look good, so this looks like a missed week, not a body problem. If work, early mornings or weather got in the way, say so in your check-in and the plan can fit around it.

## Why this week repeats the last one
Nine days off costs a new runner very little fitness, but this is not the moment to step up. Your last three walk-runs, Sep 14 – 19, went well: effort 6 to 7 out of 10, no pain, and the cough had cleared. Repeating the missed week lets you restart from there, and Saturday's extra run segment is the only step up.

## Where this is heading
Going from 2-minute runs to running the whole 5K is a big step, but you can do it if most weeks from here have all three sessions. If this week goes well, the run segments get longer next week and keep growing each week. The aim is about 20 minutes of non-stop running by late October, then building toward the full distance.

## Why there are no speed sessions
This is meant to be the phase where harder sessions come in, but for you the hard work is making the run segments longer, not running faster. Intervals or tempo running would add strain without helping you run the whole way. For now, each step up in running time is the week's hard session.

## Easing the pace
About half your heart-rate time on walk-runs has been in zone 3, mostly during the running bits at around 7:40 per km. That is normal for a beginner, but running slower is the easiest way to make longer segments feel manageable. At a gentle pace your race will take about 40 minutes, and running slowly the whole way still counts as running the whole way.

## The days around the runs
Keep running on Monday, Wednesday and Saturday, since it has worked for you and leaves a rest day after every run. Keep up the dog walks on the other days. They are good for you and don't need to change.
